entry.description: Linear-error clique partitions of split graphs. The primary source reports: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the main results of the author's preprint "Linear-Error Clique Partitions of Split Graphs via Structured Triangle Packing" (Erdős #81 series, Paper III): there is an absolute constant C such that every finite split graph G on n vertices satisfies |E(G)| − 2ν₃(G) ≤ n²/6 + C·n, where ν₃(G) is the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint triangles (Theorem 1.1); consequently G has a clique partition (a family of cliques covering every edge exactly once) with at most n²/6 + C·n cliques (Corollary 1.2). The quadratic coefficient 1/6 is the sharp one for split graphs. The constant C is existential and not explicit. Two ingredients of the proof, the asymptotic gap between fractional and integral triangle packings and exact triangle decompositions of dense triangle-divisible graphs, are taken from two registered formalizations (see related_formalizations). Direct AI involvement: The Lean development is AI-assisted under the author's direction and mechanically verified: no sorry, axioms limited to propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, identical elaborated statements and definitions in the Challenge and the Solution. Contributed, under the author's direction, the Lean proofs of the freeze lean_v1.4_freeze (Lean 4.28) from formal statements and proof plans.  Ported the 29-module core of the freeze to Lean v4.35.0-rc3 and the module system, rewriting the proofs broken by the Mathlib update; replaced the vendored Nibble, BKLO and Ax2 developments (about 360 modules) by bridges to the two registered formalizations (PaperIII/ReuseFinal.lean, PaperIII/YusterBridgeReuse.lean); wrote the Challenge/Solution pair and the packaging. Checked with a local build of the whole dependency chain, a comparison of the elaborated Challenge and Solution statements and definitions (pp.all), and #print axioms (Lean v4.35.0-rc3, Mathlib c55e6e786f49471c72fbddbec5415808896aec1e). Further checking: Only split graphs and existential linear error Cn; not all graphs or an explicit C. Resolve earlier preprint date and AI mathematics versus formalization. Independently check correctness, novelty, priority, exact AI mathematical contribution and paper-to-formal-statement correspondence. Owner/agent and registry checks are not independent expert verification; no proof artifact, program, certificate or macro was executed. Determine earliest public availability: registry registration is the dated public observation used here, not proof that earlier preparation commits or manuscripts were already public. Keep provisional=1, low strict confidence, taxonomy unreviewed and no strict Superhuman override.

entry.description: Complete-split extremizers for the fractional triangle-cover deficit on chordal graphs. The primary source reports: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the main result of the author's preprint "Complete-Split Extremizers for a Fractional Triangle-Cover Functional on Chordal Graphs" (Erdős #81 series, Paper II). For a finite simple graph G let τ₃*(G) be its fractional triangle cover number (the least total weight of a nonnegative weighting of vertex pairs giving every triangle weight at least one on its edges) and Φ_τ(G) = |E(G)| − 2τ₃*(G). For every n ≥ 1, every chordal graph on n vertices satisfies Φ_τ(G) ≤ ⌊(2n + 1)²/24⌋, and equality is attained by a complete-split graph K_p ∨ K̄_q with p + q = n (Theorem 1.2). Chordality and fractional triangle covers use the definitions of two registered entries. entry.description: CONDITIONAL on Perelli-Pintz-Salerno 1984 and Perelli-Pintz 1993: Halupczok's ternary Goldbach mean value theorem with primes in progressions and short intervals, repaired. The primary source reports: CONDITIONAL on two cited results, both taken as explicit hypotheses of the theorems and never as axioms: PPS1984Remark, the printed Remark on p. 530 of A. Perelli, J. Pintz and S. Salerno, Bombieri's theorem in short intervals, 1984, and PP1993Goldbach, the Goldbach analogue of Theorem 3 of A. Perelli and J. Pintz, On the exceptional set for Goldbach's problem in short intervals, 1993, established in its sections 3 to 5 but not printed as a numbered theorem. These are the inputs that the paper's own proof quotes as its Theorems 2.1 and 2.3. PP1993Goldbach is therefore a weaker citation than a numbered theorem: it is the unnumbered Goldbach analogue that Halupczok says the proof of Perelli and Pintz can be adapted to give, stated here in the general form that argument yields. Under the two hypotheses, a complete Lean 4 proof of a repaired form of Theorem 1.2 of K. Halupczok, Goldbach's problem with primes in arithmetic progressions and in short intervals, J. Theor. Nombres Bordeaux 25, 2013, 331 to 351: summed over moduli q <= Q, the weighted count of p1 + p2 + p3 = n with p1 = a mod q and p1, p2 in short intervals differs from its singular series main term T(n, q, a) Y1 Y2 by << Y1 Y2 L^-A. As printed, the theorem sums over all q <= Q with the printed T, which does not vanish when a and q have a common factor, while the prime sum then is empty, so the printed statement fails, for example at a = 3, q = 3. The repair takes the main term to be 0 for such q, or equivalently restricts to q coprime to a. The entry also proves that the two hypotheses imply the paper's Theorems 2.1 and 2.3, as derived results of this entry. Binary Goldbach is open and is not claimed; ternary Goldbach is a theorem of Helfgott. An AI agent wrote the Lean code; the statements were checked against the sources by an AI agent and are offered for human audit. No human expert has reviewed the mathematics. Autonomous agents wrote every lab Lean file, ran lake build, read the paper and the two cited sources from page images, and ran separate AI subagents as statement checkers; Lean 4 v4.35.0-rc3, Mathlib v4.35.0-rc3. Further checking: The qualifying contribution is the explicit a=q=3 obstruction and coprimality repair, conditional on PPS1984Remark and the unnumbered PP1993Goldbach analogue. taxonomy.claim: The source reports: CONDITIONAL on two cited results, both taken as explicit hypotheses of the theorems and never as axioms: PPS1984Remark, the printed Remark on p. 530 of A. Perelli, J. Pintz and S. Salerno, Bombieri's theorem in short intervals, 1984, and PP1993Goldbach, the Goldbach analogue of Theorem 3 of A. Perelli and J. Pintz, On the exceptional set for Goldbach's problem in short intervals, 1993, established in its sections 3 to 5 but not printed as a numbered theorem. These are the inputs that the paper's own proof quotes as its Theorems 2.1 and 2.3. PP1993Goldbach is therefore a weaker citation than a numbered theorem: it is the unnumbered Goldbach analogue that Halupczok says the proof of Perelli and Pintz can be adapted to give, stated here in the general form that argument yields. Under the two hypotheses, a complete Lean 4 proof of a repaired form of Theorem 1.2 of K. Halupczok, Goldbach's problem with primes in arithmetic progressions and in short intervals, J. Theor. Nombres Bordeaux 25, 2013, 331 to 351: summed over moduli q <= Q, the weighted count of p1 + p2 + p3 = n with p1 = a mod q and p1, p2 in short intervals differs from its singular series main term T(n, q, a) Y1 Y2 by << Y1 Y2 L^-A. As printed, the theorem sums over all q <= Q with the printed T, which does not vanish when a and q have a common factor, while the prime sum then is empty, so the printed statement fails, for example at a = 3, q = 3. The repair takes the main term to be 0 for such q, or equivalently restricts to q coprime to a. The entry also proves that the two hypotheses imply the paper's Theorems 2.1 and 2.3, as derived results of this entry. Binary Goldbach is open and is not claimed; ternary Goldbach is a theorem of Helfgott. An AI agent wrote the Lean code; the statements were checked against the sources by an AI agent and are offered for human audit.

entry.description: Zero-Sum Quartet Incidence and Sharp Maximal-Independent-Set Witnesses on Eight Vertices. The primary source reports: We prove an exact four-term probability law for zero-sum maximal-independent-set witnesses. For every connected simple graph G on eight vertices and every admissible eight-point cap U in F_3^3, sample uniformly from all 40,320 bijections of the vertices onto U. Let N0 count zero-sum maximal independent four-sets, m count the size-four maximal independent sets, n0 and n2 count their unordered pairs intersecting in zero and two vertices, and h count compatible unordered triples. Put M1 = 2m/35, M2 = 2n0/35 + n2/315, and M3 = h/315. Then P(N0=0) = 1-M1+M2-M3, P(N0=1) = M1-2M2+3M3, P(N0=2) = M2-3M3, and P(N0=3) = M3 = h/315 <= 1/105; equality holds if and only if G is isomorphic to the spider S(2,2,2,1). In particular N0 <= 3. The theorem does not assume an external cap normal-form classification. entry.description: Linked-site block laws of all lengths identify the collapsed mutation-scaled genealogy. The primary source reports: This entry formalizes an identifiability theorem for three sampled sequences whose sites all share one random three-tip genealogy (complete linkage). A genealogy is a pair of branch lengths (u, v), where u is the height of the cherry and v is the length of the upper internal branch, together with a label in Fin 3 recording which pair of tips forms the cherry. Its law is an arbitrary finite measure that is almost everywhere supported on nonnegative branch lengths. Given the genealogy, sites evolve independently under the K-state equal-rates mutation model with a uniform root distribution and mutation scale k. For K ≥ 2 and k, l ≥ 0, two such measures, with scales k and l, produce the same law of block patterns for every number L of linked sites if and only if their collapsed objects agree. The collapsed object is the push-forward of the measure under (u, v, q) ↦ (k u, k v, q), with the cherry label replaced by a fixed value whenever k v = 0. A second statement shows that, for a genealogy with zero upper branch (a star tree), the block-pattern law does not depend on which cherry label is attached. What this formalization adds is the exact identification statement for a mixture over genealogies of linked-site block laws, the explicit collapsed object that it identifies, and the star-tree label invariance, together with a proof that runs as follows. entry.description: A prespecified betting test of panmixia against a two-deme history: size and power. The primary source reports: This entry formalizes a prespecified fixed-sample test, based on independent blocks of three linked sites observed at three sampled tips with four allelic states, of a panmictic null model against a two-deme alternative. Under the null, the three-tip genealogy follows the coalescent with a time-varying pair-coalescence rate r, and sites mutate under the four-state equal-rates model with scale k. For every nonnegative locally integrable rate r whose integrated clock diverges and every k > 0, the rejection probability with at least 72,000,000,000 independent blocks is at most 1/20. For one specific two-island alternative, with all three tips sampled in the same deme, the rejection probability is at least 4/5 with exactly 72,000,000,000 blocks and at least 19/20 with exactly 250,000,000,000 blocks. The test, its features, its betting factors, its localization tolerance, and its threshold are fixed numerical choices given in the Challenge. Direct AI involvement: This repository is published by Cenozoic Works, an organization; X. Lee and N. Volkov, members of Cenozoic Works, are the responsible authors and maintainers and take responsibility for these results. Cenozoic Works directed the project and chose which results to formalize and submit; X. Lee approved the statements and this metadata. The Lean code and most of the prose were drafted by AI agents. The test, its numerical constants, and the size and power proofs were written in this project; no published source is formalized. Novelty unknown; no claim of priority. The models are standard: the three-lineage coalescent with a time-varying coalescence rate, the structured coalescent for two islands with symmetric migration, and the equal-rates mutation model; no cited source is formalized for them. The general idea of rejecting when the product of nonnegative betting factors reaches 1/alpha comes from the testing-by-betting literature cited below as context. What is specific to this entry is the following: a fixed table of five block features; a quadratic score of the five feature means, proved nonpositive under every panmictic null in the stated class; betting factors linear in the features and centred at the alternative's feature means; a localization condition that the first three empirical feature means lie within 1/100000 of the alternative's values; and explicit finite-sample size and power bounds. The size proof combines Markov's inequality for the product wealth at a fixed sample size, which applies when the null feature means lie near the alternative's values, with a Hoeffding-type concentration bound for the localization event otherwise. The power proof combines the same concentration bound with first and second moment bounds on the log wealth. entry.description: An upper bound on the denominators of solutions of the two-locus sampling recursion. The primary source reports: This entry formalizes degree and divisibility facts about the denominators of solutions to the two-locus sampling recursion with two alleles at each locus. Centred moments of a solution, grouped in blocks by the numbers i and j of lineages at the two loci, satisfy a tridiagonal linear system with matrix T(i, j) whose right-hand side involves only smaller blocks. An explicit product D of linear factors in the mutation rates and of block determinants E(p, s) = det T(p, s) clears the denominator of the solution: D times the solution lies in any subring that contains the parameters. Conditionally on D being the reduced denominator of the top centred moment, every denominator of the solution is divisible by E. The determinant E(i, j) has degree min(i, j) in the recombination rate when a nonvanishing condition holds, and is positive when i, j ≥ 2 and the rates are nonnegative. Two statements show that the diagonal determinants E(m, m), with one mutation rate set to zero, have irreducible factors of unbounded degree as m varies, both as polynomials in the mutation rate over rational functions of the recombination rate and as polynomials in the recombination rate over rational functions of the mutation rate. An explicit product D of linear factors in the mutation rates and of block determinants E(p, s) = det T(p, s) clears the denominator of the solution: D times the solution lies in any subring that contains the parameters. Conditionally on D being the reduced denominator of the top centred moment, every denominator of the solution is divisible by E. The determinant E(i, j) has degree min(i, j) in the recombination rate when a nonvanishing condition holds, and is positive when i, j ≥ 2 and the rates are nonnegative. Two statements show that the diagonal determinants E(m, m), with one mutation rate set to zero, have irreducible factors of unbounded degree as m varies, both as polynomials in the mutation rate over rational functions of the recombination rate and as polynomials in the recombination rate over rational functions of the mutation rate.

entry.description: An explicit block-recursive formula for solutions of the two-locus sampling recursion. The primary source reports: This entry formalizes an explicit block-recursive formula for the solution of the two-locus sampling recursion under parent-independent mutation, with two alleles at each locus, positive mutation rates, and nonnegative recombination rate, over any ordered field. The explicit expression equals every solution of the recursion and is itself a solution, so it is the unique solution. Lumping statements show that merging alleles, by pushing configurations forward along maps between allele sets of any sizes, carries solutions to solutions, and that when every allele class is merged into two classes the lumped values are given by the explicit two-allele formula at the merged allele frequencies. A variant of the explicit formula, for any number of alleles at one locus and two at the other, is shown to equal every solution of the recursion. (5), here specialized to parent-independent mutation and written in the killed form described under status.scope. Usmani (1994) supplies the closed-form inverse of a tridiagonal matrix that the formulas use; that identity is proved in the library, not assumed. entry.description: Block determinants of the two-locus sampling recursion: degree, positivity, squarefreeness, coprimality, and Galois groups. The primary source reports: This entry formalizes algebraic properties of the block determinants E(i, j) of the two-locus sampling recursion, viewed as polynomials in the recombination rate ρ. E(i, j) is the determinant of an explicit (min(i, j) + 1)-square tridiagonal matrix whose entries depend on i, j, the mutation rates θ_A and θ_B, and ρ. Its degree in ρ is min(i, j) under a stated nondegeneracy condition, and it is positive for i, j ≥ 2 with nonnegative parameters. For nonnegative real mutation rates, every root in ρ of E(5, 5) and of E(7, 7) is real and negative. At explicit rational parameters with negative θ_A, E(5, 5) and E(7, 7) are irreducible over the rationals, have 3 and 5 real roots, have Galois groups of orders 120 and 5040 (the full symmetric groups), and have roots that are not expressible by radicals. E(5, 5) and E(7, 7) are irreducible over the field of rational functions in the mutation rate, and their Galois groups over the field of rational functions in two independent mutation rates are the full symmetric groups; a general specialization lemma used for this is also stated. Squarefreeness, and coprimality for distinct index pairs, of the determinants with i, j ≥ 1 are stated over a field of rational functions in two independent mutation rates and over a field of Laurent series in which both mutation rates are large with a ratio that is not rational. Direct AI involvement: This repository is published by Cenozoic Works, an organization; X. Lee and N. Volkov, members of Cenozoic Works, are the responsible authors and maintainers and take responsibility for these results. Cenozoic Works directed the project and chose which results to formalize and submit; X. Lee approved the statements and this metadata. The Lean code and most of the prose were drafted by AI agents. Results are attributed to models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, internal models, and human experts. Every proof is checked by the Lean kernel. Agents worked in a Lean 4 and Mathlib toolchain with Lake, the Lean compiler, and the repository's build and checking scripts. They drafted the definitions, statements, and proofs, ported modules between toolchain versions, and repaired build errors.  Agents searched the literature, read the cited sources, and drafted the source notes and the informal account in this file. Further checking: Primary owner describes an original result relative to its cited sources, but explicitly makes no priority certification. Treat established model/recursion/moment machinery as background, not new discoveries. Exact model hypotheses and source-to-proof correspondence need independent audit. Novelty unknown; no claim of priority. None of the listed sources supplies the determinants or the results. In this entry E(i, j) is defined directly as the determinant of an explicit tridiagonal matrix, so no statement depends on a source for the recursion; within this repository the same matrix is the within-block system of the two-locus sampling recursion under parent-independent mutation that the ExplicitFormula entry inverts block by block. What this formalization presents relative to the cited sources is the set of statements in status.scope: the ρ-degree, positivity, real-rootedness with negative roots for (5, 5) and (7, 7), irreducibility and full symmetric Galois groups of E(5, 5) and E(7, 7) at explicit rational parameters and over rational-function fields, non-solvability by radicals at those parameters, and squarefreeness and coprimality over generic and Laurent-series fields. Standard results proved in Mathlib (the prime-degree criterion for a full symmetric Galois group, the Abel–Ruffini criterion, and the theory of decomposition groups) are used as tools and are listed under related_formalizations. entry.description: Linked-pair panels: panel laws are determined by finitely many Laplace values. The primary source reports: This entry formalizes panels of linked site pairs observed through a reporting channel, with the pair coalescence time T following a probability law on the non-negative reals. All L sites of a panel share the same time T; given T = t, the sites are reported independently, and at each site the two lineages share one latent type with weight e^(−kt) and have independent types otherwise, each type being reported through a channel that maps K latent types to probability distributions on a finite set of labels. For an informative channel (one whose rows are not all equal) and a panel of length L, the panel laws of two time laws agree for all outcomes if and only if their Laplace transforms agree at the points rk for r = 0, …, L. If the channel erases all information, every panel law agrees. If the transforms agree up to L and differ at the next point, then panels of length L agree but some panel of length L + 1 differs. For k > 0, agreement of all panels of all lengths is equivalent to equality of the time laws. Direct AI involvement: This repository is published by Cenozoic Works, an organization; X. Lee and N. Volkov, members of Cenozoic Works, are the responsible authors and maintainers and take responsibility for these results. The four compared theorems are presented in this formalization: the exact finite-length criterion (for an informative channel, panel laws of length L agree exactly when the Laplace values at rk, r = 0, …, L, agree), the erased-channel case, the sharp step from length L to length L + 1, and identification of the time law from panels of all lengths. Relative to the cited sources, what is new here is the reporting-channel setting, the exact equivalence at each finite length, and its sharpness; the cited works express probabilities of sequence data through Laplace transforms or generating functions of coalescence times, and the classical uniqueness theorem for the Hausdorff moment problem supplies the established mathematics behind all_panels_eq_iff. All L sites of a panel share the same time T; given T = t, the sites are reported independently, and at each site the two lineages share one latent type with weight e^(−kt) and have independent types otherwise, each type being reported through a channel that maps K latent types to probability distributions on a finite set of labels. For an informative channel (one whose rows are not all equal) and a panel of length L, the panel laws of two time laws agree for all outcomes if and only if their Laplace transforms agree at the points rk for r = 0, …, L. If the channel erases all information, every panel law agrees. If the transforms agree up to L and differ at the next point, then panels of length L agree but some panel of length L + 1 differs. For k > 0, agreement of all panels of all lengths is equivalent to equality of the time laws.

entry.description: No formula with denominators of bounded degree, in the total mutation parameter or in rho, for the two-locus sampling recursion. The primary source reports: This entry formalizes results on the degree of denominators of any closed-form expression for the solution of the two-locus sampling recursion of the coalescent with recombination, with two alleles at each locus and parent-independent mutation. The mutation rates, the recombination rate rho, and the allele frequencies are independent indeterminates, and the recursion is solved over a field of rational functions in them. An expression is built from rational constants, arbitrary coefficients from the coefficient field, the rates, sums, products, and quotients; it is admissible at degree D when every divisor evaluates to a nonzero polynomial of degree at most D in a designated variable (rho, or the total mutation rate theta_A + theta_B). A closure lemma shows that admissible expressions in inputs with bounded denominators have bounded denominators. For the sample of two lineages that carry the same haplotype at both loci, no admissible expression of degree one in rho, and none of degree two in the total mutation rate, equals the value of the solution; variants bound the total degree of the divisors in the three rates instead. For the samples of m lineages typed at locus A only and m typed at locus B only, all of allele 0, for every bound D there is an m ≥ 2 at which no admissible expression of degree D, in the total mutation rate or in rho, equals the value of the solution. Existence and uniqueness of the solutions are also stated in these settings. Direct AI involvement: This repository is published by Cenozoic Works, an organization; X. Lee and N. Agents searched the literature, read the cited sources, and drafted the source notes and the informal account in this file. The non-existence statements are presented here for the first time as far as this record knows; no literature search establishing that is claimed. Novelty unknown; no claim of priority. The established mathematics that the entry builds on is the two-locus sampling recursion under parent-independent mutation, in the finite-allele form given by Bhaskar and Song (2012) and treated by Jenkins and Song (2012), with the infinite-alleles form going back to Golding (1984) and Ethier and Griffiths (1990); the closed forms for a sample of size two at total mutation rate 0 (Durrett 2008, Simonsen and Churchill 1997) are context for the block-(2,2) statements. Formulated for this formalization: the classes of admissible expressions (with the designated degree variable and arbitrary coefficient leaves), the closure lemma for bounded denominators, the identification of an irreducible denominator factor of the value at the two-haplotype sample (degree two in rho, degree three in the total mutation rate), the existence and uniqueness proofs over the fields of rational functions, and the statements for the families indexed by m. entry.description: A partition-pair decomposition of the two-locus sampling probability with Ewens marginals. The primary source reports: This entry formalizes a decomposition of the two-locus sampling probability, under finite-allele parent-independent mutation, in terms of pairs of set partitions of the sample, with Ewens marginals at each locus. A partition-carrying ancestral process with coalescence, mutation, and recombination records, at each locus, which sample members lose their ancestry to the same mutation; the kernel is the probability that it ends with a given pair of partitions. The solution of the two-locus sampling recursion at a fully typed sample is the sum over pairs of partitions of the kernel times the probability that each block receives a single allele consistent with the sample. Summing the kernel over the partition at one locus gives the Ewens partition probability at the other; as the recombination rate tends to infinity the kernel tends to the product of the two Ewens partition probabilities; and with recombination rate 0 the common refinement of the two partitions has the Ewens law with parameter θA + θB. The sampling probability equals the product of its one-locus marginals for all parameter values exactly when at most one lineage is typed at one of the loci (with at least two alleles per locus). A closed form for configurations with two lineages typed at each locus is also stated, together with existence of a solution of the recursion. entry.description: Seven linked sites separate a two-island history from every panmictic history. The primary source reports: This entry formalizes a statement about blocks of seven completely linked sites with K ≥ 2 equally weighted roots, observed in three sampled sequences under an equal-rates K-state mutation model. A specific two-island history for three lineages (all three lineages start in the same island, the coalescence rate within an island is 1, and the migration rate is 1/100) produces, at mutation scale 1, a law of the seven-site block that differs from the block law of every panmictic history at every mutation scale k > 0. The panmictic histories are those given by a nonnegative locally integrable pairwise coalescence rate whose integrated clock diverges, so the population size may vary arbitrarily in time. entry.description: Total variation bound between an unpruned ancestral recombination process and SMC' on pairwise coalescence times. The primary source reports: This entry formalizes a total variation bound between the pairwise coalescence-time process of an unpruned ancestral recombination graph and the SMC' approximation, for N ≥ 1 samples, a unit-length genome, and scaled recombination rate R ≥ 0. The observed object is the collection of pairwise coalescence times of all sample pairs at every rational position in [0, 1). The total variation distance is at most an explicit double bound, which is at most min(1, R² times a quadratic coefficient in N − 1). The distance is 0 for one sample and for zero recombination. Supporting statements show that the event kernels of both processes are Markov, the two laws are probability measures, the number of live lineages of the backward process reaches at most one almost surely, the observed coalescence times are almost surely finite, and the expected number of active events, the expected total time, and the expected largest observed coalescence time are bounded by an explicit absorption budget. The established mathematics the entry builds on is the coalescent with recombination (ancestral recombination graph), for which Griffiths and Durrett are listed as background, and the SMC' algorithm of Marjoram and Wall, whose spatial construction the Lean definitions implement. challengeContext.anchorClaim: The source reports: This entry formalizes a total variation bound between the pairwise coalescence-time process of an unpruned ancestral recombination graph and the SMC' approximation, for N ≥ 1 samples, a unit-length genome, and scaled recombination rate R ≥ 0. The observed object is the collection of pairwise coalescence times of all sample pairs at every rational position in [0, 1). The total variation distance is at most an explicit double bound, which is at most min(1, R² times a quadratic coefficient in N − 1). The distance is 0 for one sample and for zero recombination. Supporting statements show that the event kernels of both processes are Markov, the two laws are probability measures, the number of live lineages of the backward process reaches at most one almost surely, the observed coalescence times are almost surely finite, and the expected number of active events, the expected total time, and the expected largest observed coalescence time are bounded by an explicit absorption budget.

entry.description: When one finite block of linked sites separates a three-sample genealogy from every panmictic history. The primary source reports: This entry formalizes conditions under which a single finite block of linked sites separates a three-sample genealogy from every panmictic history. A law of the two coalescence-interval lengths and the tree shape of three sampled sequences is uniformly separated at mutation scale k > 0 when some block of L completely linked sites, observed under the equal-rates mutation model, has a law at ℓ1 distance at least a fixed ε > 0 from the block law of every panmictic history (any nonnegative, locally integrable, time-varying coalescence rate with a diverging integrated clock), at every mutation scale and for every alphabet size K ≥ 2. For laws with nonnegative interval lengths, a positive first coalescence time, and a regular first-survival profile matching the first coalescence time, uniform separation holds if and only if the law differs from the panmictic law with the profile's rate, in which the tree shape is uniform and independent of the times; a version for laws of the interval lengths alone, with a uniform independent shape, is also given. For three-sample symmetric island histories with time-varying coalescence and migration rates under the stated integrability hypotheses, uniform separation holds if and only if the history is not the one with all three lineages starting in the same island, no migration, and a diverging integrated coalescence clock. For finite-phase histories, separation is equivalent to failure of a density identity characterizing the panmictic form. entry.description: SmallRatio: Dedekind sums along Euclid's algorithm and the small-ratio formula. The primary source reports: For a prime p and 0 < h < p, the Dedekind sum s(h,p) is determined, up to an explicit error of order log p, by the fractions of small height congruent to plus or minus h: with the sum over the coprime pairs u, v >= 1 with uv < p/2, |12 s(h,p) - p sum ([hv = u mod p] - [hv = -u mod p])/(uv)| <= 6n <= 12 log_2 p + 6, where n is the length of Euclid's algorithm on (p, h). Summed over any set H of residues, in particular over a subgroup of odd order, this gives |12 sum_{h in H} s(h,p) - p S_H(p)| <= |H| (12 log_2 p + 6), where S_H(p) is the signed sum of 1/(uv) over the coprime pairs with uv < p/2 and u/v in H or -H. The development proves Dedekind reciprocity from scratch (by counting lattice points), the identities of Euclid's algorithm and the bound n <= 2 log_2 k + 1, the alternating-sum form 12 s(h,k) = sum (-1)^{j+1} k/(r_j q_{j-1}) + E with |E| <= 4n, and Legendre's pairing of the small coprime pairs with the steps of the algorithm, by a lattice-basis argument instead of continued fractions. The scope (the Dedekind-sum form, with Proposition 5.1 quoted) and the lattice proof of Legendre's pairing were chosen during formalization to keep the development elementary. entry.description: Short sums of certain arithmetic functions (Nair–Tenenbaum). The primary source reports: Reports a checked arithmetic counterexample for Q=X to the printed Lemma1, a constant-unit-coordinate counterexample requiring nonconstancy in Corollary6, and corrected totient/selected-prime comparisons. Main short-sum theorems retain their coefficient/discriminant uniformity; this is a scoped correction, not a new discovery of the1998 theorems. The main theorems retain their stated coefficient and discriminant uniformity. Arithmetic functions are defined on positive tuples and extended by zero at a zero polynomial value, making otherwise undefined terms explicit. Polynomial factorization data are supplied in the compared statements and constructed in additional library interfaces. Theorem 2 explicitly assumes positive polynomial degree and fixes the integer k before choosing its threshold. The o(1) exponents in the Hooley corollaries are expressed by every coefficient eta strictly greater than the stated limiting coefficient, with corresponding thresholds. Corollary 6 requires positive degree of the restricted coordinate; a checked constant-unit-coordinate example shows the saving can otherwise fail. Corollary 7 corrects the printed transposed interval condition to x^(4 epsilon) <= y <= x. Corollary 9 makes explicit the range 1 <= |a| <= x inherited from Corollary 8, hence applies eventually to each fixed nonzero residue. The printed Lemma 1 is refuted by a checked arithmetic counterexample for Q=X; the totient and selected-prime comparisons actually used by the main proofs are proved separately. The proof of Theorem 1 replaces a single-gcd removal by removal of whole bad prime powers. The proof of Theorem 3 handles the small fixed primes that adjoining X can introduce. entry.description: Proof of WOWII Conjecture 96 (DeLaVina, Graffiti.pc). The primary source reports: A Lean 4 proof of Conjecture 96 of Written on the Wall II (Graffiti.pc): every connected graph G on at least two vertices satisfies α(G) ≤ 1 + min_v disteven(v)·(max_v l(v) − 1), where disteven(v) is the number of vertices at even distance from v and l(v) is the independence number of the neighbourhood of v. entry.description: The two-qubit Hardy ladder: the closed form P_K*(q) and its unique maximiser for every K, Hardy's optimum at K = 1, and the optimum (8 rho^2 + rho - 11)/25 in the cubic field Q(rho) at K = 2. The primary source reports: Kernel-checked optimum of Hardy's K-step ladder for two qubits (Hardy 1993; Hardy 1997; Boschi, Branca, De Martini and Hardy 1997), for a real Schmidt state c0|00> + c1|11> and real projective settings, the probabilities written out as squared real amplitudes. For every K: under the ladder constraints P(A_K = 1, B_K = 1) <= q^2 (1 - q^{2K})^2 / ((1 + q^2)(1 + q^{2K+1})^2), q = c1/c0, with equality attained (Cereceda 2002, eqs. (18)-(19)); the probability is below 1/2 (the two-qubit, real-settings case of a bound that follows in every dimension from Cereceda 2016, eq. (9), with Wehner 2006), and for every eps > 0 and every large enough K some state and settings exceed 1/2 - eps (the "(50 - delta)%" of Hardy 1997 and Boschi et al. 1997). For every K >= 1 the maximiser of the closed form on (0, 1) is the unique zero there of Cereceda's polynomial m_K (Cereceda 2002, eq. (20), stated there without proof): the derivative of the closed form, the existence and uniqueness of the zero, the maximum and its uniqueness, and, over all Schmidt states and real settings, the optimum, its attainment at the Schmidt ratio r, and that every optimal configuration has Schmidt ratio r or 1/r (attainment at 1/r follows from the uncompared symmetry). Worked instances: the K = 1 optimum is phi^{-5} = (5 sqrt 5 - 11)/2 (Hardy 1993), attained at a state with 2 c0 c1 = 3 - sqrt 5 and only where 2 c0 c1 = 3 - sqrt 5 (Hardy's condition); the K = 2 optimum is (8 rho^2 + rho - 11)/25 = 0.17455..., rho the plastic number (the real root of x^3 - x - 1), attained at Schmidt weights c0^2 = rho^{-1}, c1^2 = rho^{-5} (c1/c0 = rho^{-2}) and only where {c0^2, c1^2} = {rho^{-1}, rho^{-5}}. The value 0.17455 is in print numerically; the closed form, the maximiser rho^{-2}, the weights and the minimal polynomial 25x^3 + 17x^2 + 2x - 1 of the value were not found in the literature searched (2026-10-28) and are the entry's new content. Also: the K = 2 value is not totally real (its minimal polynomial has a non-real complex root). Optimality over complex settings is not formalised. Thirty compared statements. Every theorem kernel-checked and axiom-audited (AxiomAudit.lean: #print axioms for all 160 library theorems and the thirty compared theorems). Statements 1-2, 12-15, 19-23 and 27-29 and the first seven library modules were drafted with Claude Fable 5.1; HardyLadder/Optimum.lean, HardyLadder/OneHalf.lean, HardyLadder/Maximiser.lean, the last section of HardyLadder/TotallyReal.lean, statements 3-11, 16-18, 24-26 and 30, and later text edits with Claude Opus 5.5. entry.description:
PCF all the way down. The primary source reports: Let k be a field of characteristic zero and let f: X → X be a finite surjective map of integral k-schemes of finite type. By the critical locus of f we mean the image in X of the critical locus of the map induced on the normalization of X. By the branch locus we mean the image of the critical locus under f.

We say that f is post-critically finite (PCF) if, for every irreducible divisor D contained in the branch locus, the forward orbit f(D) ∪ f^2(D) ∪ … is algebraic, that is, a finite union of subvarieties, taken as a closed subscheme with its reduced induced structure.

We prove that if f is PCF and A is a preperiodic divisor for f with f^{r+s}(A) = f^r(A), then, setting B = f^r(A) and g = f^s, the restriction of g to B is PCF.

This proves the PCF all the way down conjecture: restricting again to preperiodic divisors and iterating gives PCF maps at every stage.
 Direct AI involvement: Claude Code CLI with Anthropic models and OpenAI Codex desktop with OpenAI models, as recorded in the parent project's formalization.yaml. The underlying development predates this target-specific package.

challengeContext.anchorClaim:
The source reports: Let k be a field of characteristic zero and let f: X → X be a finite surjective map of integral k-schemes of finite type. By the critical locus of f we mean the image in X of the critical locus of the map induced on the normalization of X. By the branch locus we mean the image of the critical locus under f.

We say that f is post-critically finite (PCF) if, for every irreducible divisor D contained in the branch locus, the forward orbit f(D) ∪ f^2(D) ∪ … is algebraic, that is, a finite union of subvarieties, taken as a closed subscheme with its reduced induced structure.

We prove that if f is PCF and A is a preperiodic divisor for f with f^{r+s}(A) = f^r(A), then, setting B = f^r(A) and g = f^s, the restriction of g to B is PCF.

This proves the PCF all the way down conjecture: restricting again to preperiodic divisors and iterating gives PCF maps at every stage.

entry.description: Sharp reset thresholds for bounded-response synchronization games with a sink. The primary source reports: Lean 4 / Mathlib statements of the theorem M(n,k) = sum_{i=1}^{n-1} ceil(i/k) for k = 1 or n <= k+3 (Lipin-Volkov k-game on automata with a sink), rendered as an upper and a lower bound, with the headline case M(5,2) = 6, proved in Solution.lean from the development SinkReset.Plan written in the conductor formalize run 2026-10-25_formalize-sinkresetthresholds. The endpoints k = 1 (Rystsov's tight bound n(n-1)/2) and k = n-1 were known from Lipin-Volkov; the new content is M(k+2,k) = k+2 and M(k+3,k) = k+4 for k >= 2, including the non-divisible pairs (4,2) and (5,3), which the Lipin-Volkov conjecture (stated for k | n-1 only) does not cover; (5,2) is the first pair that is neither endpoint. entry.description: A finite two-temperature lower bound for the GHR sum-difference constant. The primary source reports: The Gyarmati-Hennecart-Ruzsa constant C₃ₐ is the supremum of real exponents theta for which every K > 1 admits a positive constant c and arbitrarily large nonempty finite integer sets X with nonempty partners Y satisfying |X+Y| <= K|X| and c|X+Y|^theta <= |X-Y|. This formalization proves the strict bound C₃ₐ > 60709/50000 = 1.21418. A finite type at depth 10^13, separate difference and sum tilts, cyclic compression, and a proved finite-set principle supply the bound. entry.description:
Four-cell tails after an alternating stripe in Rule 30. The primary source reports: For the zero-boundary left half started from $S_{1..m} \cdot v \cdot 0^\infty$ (the alternating stripe at depths $1, \dots, m$, then a tail $v$ of four cells, then white), the first deviation from the stripe comes at a depth $d \le m + 6$, and depth $1$ is white at some even time $t \le (d - 1) + 31$, at most 31 steps after the deviation arrives (`Rule30Submission.stripe_four_tail`). This holds for every $m$ and every tail $v \in \{0, 1\}^4$, except $v = 1011$, read outwards, with $m$ odd.

The catalog's `Rule30ZeroBoundaryStripeFamily` proves this for tails of at most three cells. The proof carries it to four by the same route, with one periodic orbit of the front window per class $(m \bmod 2,\ v)$, checked by the kernel. The exception is real: for $m = 33157$ and $v = 1011$, a direct simulation finds the first white even time at $33190$, so no bound of 31 steps holds there.

This is a partial result for one family of starts, not a proof of `Q01` or of Problem 1. The kit's catalog now has it as `Rule30ZeroBoundaryStripeFour`. entry.description:
Six-bit core exclusions at padding 74 by backward vacuum certificates. The primary source reports: For each of the sixteen six-bit Boolean words $u$ beginning and ending in black, and every $r\ge74$, no column of a Rule 30 configuration with a leftmost black cell eventually repeats $0^r u$, after any transient (`Rule30Submission.no_six_bit_core`). This includes every column of every nonzero finite starting configuration.

The result extends the contribution's five-tail framework to the new six-bit black-ended cores. Backward predecessor chains start at the vacuum and allow both right inputs at each step. entry.description:
White Padding before 10111 and Eighty-Seven Periodic Words in Rule 30. The primary source reports: For every $q \ge 9$, the single-seed Rule 30 center column is not eventually the repeating word $0^q10111$, for any transient or phase. The theorem is `Rule30Submission.WhitePad10111.not_eventually_zeros_10111`. The accompanying 87 theorems `Rule30Submission.not_eventually_<word>` exclude the explicitly listed words of lengths 12 to 16, again with arbitrary onset.

Troyusrex2's [PR #1](https://github.com/WolframInstitute/Rule30PrizeKit/pull/1), in `Rule30VacuumFiveTailsResearch.W8`, already proves the same tail family for $q \ge 62$ and covers every column of a leftmost-black start. Here the threshold improves to nine for the single-seed center. The 87 words supplement the named exclusions inspected in `Rule30StripCertificateTable`, `Rule30BlackRuns`, `Rule30BlackRunBlocks`, `Rule30WhiteRunEight` and `Rule30WhiteEnd`; the certificate method itself is prior work.

The uniform proof encloses eight-cell reachable sets in sets closed under one further white step. Three blocks enter a 24-state invariant, whose masked neighbor observation is determined by the phase. The kit's masked Jen theorem contradicts an eventual periodic driver. The 87 individual exclusions use ranking certificates and the existing strip soundness theorem.

No full prize problem is solved. Finite occurrences of these words are allowed, and no blanket historical-priority claim is made. references.title: Distinct spatial column traces with an explicit uniform bound — primary dated statement/disclosure
Primary publication and scope evidence

entry.description:
Every Run of the Center Column Is Shorter Than Its Start Time. The primary source reports: For the center column $c$ of rule 30 from a single black cell, a block of black cells that starts at time $a \ge 1$ has length at most $a$ (`Rule30Submission.black_run_le`, tight at $a = 3$), and a block of white cells that starts at time $a \ge 3$ has length at most $a - 3$ (`white_run_le_three`; at most $a - 1$ for every $a \ge 1$, `white_run_le'`, attained only at $a = 2$). The block need not be a maximal run. Hence every window $[a, 2a)$ holds a black cell and every window $[a, 2a]$ a white one (`exists_black'`, `exists_white`), and $\log_2 n + 1 \le \mathrm{blackCount}\,n$ for $n \ge 1$ (`log_two_succ_le_blackCount`, with the kit's `blackCount` from Problem 2). The black bound holds for every column of every configuration with a leftmost black cell, measured from the time the left edge passed the column (`black_run_le_evol`).

This supersedes the authors' R30-20261024-801153 (white bound $3a - 2$, base-4 counts). The catalog proves only that both colors occur infinitely often; its run-length results assume eventual periodicity. Condrey (arXiv:2609.09431) bounds the run *from time 0* of a finite start by its support radius; Herbert et al. (R30-20261022-0616de, 1d5070) bound white runs of a *row* inside the settled band of left diagonals.

The argument is locality alone. During a white run, column 1 is a step function, white until the first black cell right of the center arrives and black from then on (`first_black`, `front_moves`, `black_stays`), so left-permutivity (`cell_left`) determines the whole row left of the center by one closed form from the first step of the run (`pre_triangle`). That row cannot match the rigid diagonals $D_3 = [a \text{ odd}]$ and $D_4 = 1$ (from the kit's `D_step`) if the block reaches length $a - 2$.

The bounds are linear while observed runs look logarithmic; nothing here gives a positive density, bears on Problem 1, or is a certificate. challengeContext.anchorClaim:
The source reports: For the center column $c$ of rule 30 from a single black cell, a block of black cells that starts at time $a \ge 1$ has length at most $a$ (`Rule30Submission.black_run_le`, tight at $a = 3$), and a block of white cells that starts at time $a \ge 3$ has length at most $a - 3$ (`white_run_le_three`; at most $a - 1$ for every $a \ge 1$, `white_run_le'`, attained only at $a = 2$). The block need not be a maximal run. Hence every window $[a, 2a)$ holds a black cell and every window $[a, 2a]$ a white one (`exists_black'`, `exists_white`), and $\log_2 n + 1 \le \mathrm{blackCount}\,n$ for $n \ge 1$ (`log_two_succ_le_blackCount`, with the kit's `blackCount` from Problem 2). The black bound holds for every column of every configuration with a leftmost black cell, measured from the time the left edge passed the column (`black_run_le_evol`).

This supersedes the authors' R30-20261024-801153 (white bound $3a - 2$, base-4 counts). The catalog proves only that both colors occur infinitely often; its run-length results assume eventual periodicity. Condrey (arXiv:2609.09431) bounds the run *from time 0* of a finite start by its support radius; Herbert et al. (R30-20261022-0616de, 1d5070) bound white runs of a *row* inside the settled band of left diagonals.

The argument is locality alone. During a white run, column 1 is a step function, white until the first black cell right of the center arrives and black from then on (`first_black`, `front_moves`, `black_stays`), so left-permutivity (`cell_left`) determines the whole row left of the center by one closed form from the first step of the run (`pre_triangle`). That row cannot match the rigid diagonals $D_3 = [a \text{ odd}]$ and $D_4 = 1$ (from the kit's `D_step`) if the block reaches length $a - 2$.

The bounds are linear while observed runs look logarithmic; nothing here gives a positive density, bears on Problem 1, or is a certificate.

entry.description:
Exact XOR Superposition Rigidity for Rule 30. The primary source reports: For every two ordinary Rule 30 histories $A,B:\mathbb N\times\mathbb Z\to\{0,1\}$, their pointwise XOR is itself a Rule 30 history if and only if $A=0$, $B=0$, or $A=B$. The equalities concern complete histories, with no finite support, boundary or periodicity hypotheses. `Rule30Submission.xor_history_iff` states the recurrence explicitly; `Rule30Submission.standard_two_partners` gives exactly the two partners of every nonzero history.

The proposed kit contribution is this general superposition classification. The comparison kit, commit `2f63afda261888e04ec57237290e723190914a1d`, supplies ordinary Rule 30 evolution in `Rule30Jen` and the prize statements in `Rule30Prize`. The one-step quadratic mixed-product identity is background algebra, also noted in [Dibujaron's public Rule 30 notes](https://github.com/Dibujaron/rule30); maps commuting with Rule 30 were constrained by Coven, Hedlund and Rhodes (1979), whose map-level results do not classify individual history pairs. Historical priority for the classification is not asserted.

Encode a synchronized pair of Boolean states as a four-color vector. The local cross defect is the determinant of adjacent vectors. Strong induction on the separation between incompatible nonzero colors shows that an intervening zero gap cannot persist. Restricting at arbitrary integer roots removes the half-line boundary freedom, and a linear coordinate shear returns to ordinary Rule 30.

This is a structural partial result related to the prize, not a proof of center-column nonperiodicity, balance, or computational complexity. No quantitative collision-time bound or affine four-history classification is claimed.

entry.description: Problem 2 is exactly one nearly-geometric sequence of nearly-balanced scales. The primary source reports: Let $c(t)$ be the center column of rule 30 and $D(n)=2\,\mathrm{blackCount}(n)-n$ its discrepancy walk. We prove that Problem 2 (density $1/2$) is equivalent to the existence of a single strictly increasing sequence $g$ such that, for every $k>0$, eventually $k\,|D(g_j)|\le g_j$ and $k\,(g_{j+1}-g_j)\le g_j$. In the return-gap form of the density statement, both quantifier uniformities ($\forall k$ accuracy and $\forall m$ relative gap) are redundant; one nearly-geometric sequence of nearly-balanced scales carries the whole obligation. The proof is elementary: the $\pm1$ discrepancy walk telescopes, and a diagonalisation merges the two quantifier blocks into one sequence. The result is a new exact equivalent form of Problem 2 (`Rule30Submission.problem2_iff_singleSequence`); it is not a proof of Problem 2, and no bound on the scales or density is claimed. entry.description: Single-cell period-4 absorption for the word 0001. The primary source reports: Let $w=0001$ and let the right half of rule 30 be driven by $w^\infty$. The ether-and-wall absorption conjecture says every finitely supported right half eventually enters a fixed family of ether-aligned rows ending in a 13-cell wall; for $w=0001$ it would exclude the centre tail $0001^\infty$ and hence least period 4. We prove the single-cell case in Lean: for every position $p$ and every phase $\varphi$, the right half with one black cell at $p$ and all other cells white enters the ether-and-wall family for alignment $(5,0)$ or $(6,0)$. The proof splits into $p\ge 31$, where the cell lies outside the backward light cone of the wall window at the all-white entry time $14-\varphi$, and the finite range $1\le p\le 30$, checked by kernel computation of the row recurrence; the phase reduces to $\varphi\bmod 4$. The source is kernel-checked with only `propext` and `Quot.sound`, with no `sorry`, `native_decide` or `bv_decide`. This is a partial result for Problem 1: the single-cell restriction of the open period-4 absorption conjecture, not the full absorption statement and not a period-4 exclusion. entry.description: All finite right halves supported above 30 are absorbed by the period-4 ether-and-wall family. The primary source reports: Let $w=0001$, and let the right half of rule 30 be driven by $w^\infty$. The ether-and-wall absorption conjecture says every finitely supported right half eventually enters a fixed ether-aligned family ending in a 13-cell wall; for $w=0001$ it would exclude the centre tail $0001^\infty$ and least period 4. We prove the high-support case in Lean: every finitely supported right half that is white on positions $1,\dots,30$, of any size, enters the ether-and-wall family at time $14-\varphi$ for every phase $\varphi$. The wall window at that time is confined to cells $1,\dots,16$, which cells at positions at least 31 cannot influence at speed one, so the orbit agrees with the all-white orbit and inherits the family; the phase reduces to $\varphi\bmod4$. The source is kernel-checked with only `propext` and `Quot.sound`, with no `sorry`, `native_decide` or `bv_decide`. This is a partial result for Problem 1: an infinite family inside the open period-4 absorption conjecture, not full absorption and not a period-4 exclusion. entry.description:
The White End of Rule 30 from q = 9, by One Pumped Certificate. The primary source reports: For every $q \ge 9$, the center column of rule 30 grown from a single black cell is not eventually the repeating word $1\,0^q$, for any transient: `Rule30Submission.not_eventually_white_end_ge9` proves $\neg\,\mathrm{EventuallyWord}(1\,0^q)$ for all $q \ge 9$, and `Rule30Submission.not_eventually_zeros_one_ge9` gives the same for $0^q\,1$.

What is new: the kit's `Rule30WhiteEnd` covers $q \ge 10$ and its check fails at $q = 9$. Here one argument covers the whole family, and `Rule30WhiteEnd` is not used. A mode certificate (`Rule30Submission.not_eventually_word_mode`, sound for every word, width and phase) lets column $1$ of a twelve-cell strip relaxation carry one free bit per period, a label fixed by the strip. If a label $1$ is always followed by $0$, and two $0$s by a $0$, then the labels are eventually 2-periodic and masked Jen applies. For $1\,0^q$ the certificate is one formula in $q$. For every $q \ge 10$ it follows from one $q$-independent check of sets closed under white steps (pumping over the white run). At $q = 9$, where label $1$ occurs, the kernel evaluates the same formula; a Lean evaluation shows that the same pumped check fails when started at nine white steps.

Nothing is claimed for $1\,0^q$ with $q \le 8$, for other words, or for Problem 1.

entry.description:
Short Blocks Before Long White Runs in the Center Column of Rule 30. The primary source reports: For the single-seed evolution of rule 30, the center column is not eventually a repeated word consisting of any Boolean block of at most nine cells followed by at least 102 white cells, whatever the transient. The theorem `Rule30Submission.not_eventually_short` states this for every block and every such white-tail length. A second theorem, `Rule30Submission.not_eventually_reset_mixtures`, excludes repeated concatenations of isolated black cells whose white gaps are all at least 9 and include a gap of at least 17.

Relative to the pinned kit catalog, the first family extends the padded-word theorem from tails of at most six cells to tails of at most nine, preserving the earlier sharper bounds. The second family includes mixtures containing gaps of exactly 9.

A sparse graph with checked return ranks and word budgets then forces the relevant observation, contradicting masked Jen. Primary publication and scope evidence

entry.description:
Long White Runs in the Center Column of Rule 30. The primary source reports: For the single-seed evolution of rule 30, the center column is not eventually a repeating word whose white runs all have length at least 17, whatever the transient. The theorem covers every nonempty list of blocks $1^{r_i}0^{q_i}$ with $r_i\ge1$ and $q_i\ge17$, independently chosen. A second family excludes arbitrary mixtures of single black cells followed by at least ten white cells and double black cells followed by at least eight. Isolated ones are a special case.

The proof uses a fourteen-cell strip with an arbitrary right boundary. Two blocks capture every strip into an envelope of 683 states. Nine rank regions ensure that rank eventually stabilizes; rank-preserving blocks then force column one on every white run, contradicting masked Jen. All finite inclusions are evaluated by the Lean kernel. A proved-sound bit-parallel image checker accelerates the same transitions; one module contains the entire long-white certificate.

The pure-black-tail consequence is exposed in the existing padded-word interface: every tail of at least three black cells has white-padding bound 17, retaining all sharper existing bounds. The families extend several catalog exclusions, with overlapping singleton cases. They do not settle Problem 1.

Primary publication and scope evidence

entry.description:
A Four-Category Block Grammar for the Center Column of Rule 30. The primary source reports: For the single-seed evolution of rule 30, the center column is not eventually periodic with a period made of blocks $1^r 0^q$ drawn from four run categories, for any transient: `Rule30Submission.not_eventually_grammar` proves $\neg\,\mathrm{EventuallyWord}(1^{r_1}0^{q_1}\cdots 1^{r_k}0^{q_k})$ for every nonempty list in which each block, chosen independently, has $r = 1, q \ge 10$; $r = 2, q \ge 8$; $r = 4, q \ge 7$; or $r \ge 9, q \ge 9$.

What is new: the kit excludes periods whose black runs all have length at least 9, a long black run followed by a dominating white run, $1\,0^q$ for $q \ge 10$, and $0^r u$ for short tails $u$. None covers periods that mix long black runs with blocks of one, two or four black cells and white runs of 7 to 16 cells, such as $1^4 0^7 1^{12} 0^9 1\,0^{10}$. For $1^4 0^q$ the kit needs $q \ge 49$.

Method: a fourteen-cell strip envelope captures every admissible block in four stages ($16384 \to 2288 \to 1915 \to 1797 \to 1791$ strips). Seven rank regions that no block can raise make the rank eventually constant; then column $1$ is forced on every white run, contradicting masked Jen. All finite checks reside in one family-data module; transition inclusions use a bit-parallel checker proved sound for every width.

Nothing is claimed for periods containing a block with $r = 3$ or $5 \le r \le 8$, or for Problem 1.

entry.description:
A Half-Rate Exponent Bound for Right-Diagonal Periods in Rule 30. The primary source reports: For Rule 30 grown from one black cell, let $R(j,t)=\mathrm{cell}(t,t-j)$. For every $j,t\ge0$, we prove $R(j,t+2^{B(j)})=R(j,t)$ (`Rule30Submission.right_period`), where $B(j)=\lceil j/2\rceil+Q_0(\lfloor j/2\rfloor)$. Here $Q_0(d)$ counts records at most $d$ in $R_0(1)=1$, $R_0(q+1)=R_0(q)+2^{R_0(q)+q-1}$. The exact integer bound is formalized; $B(j)=j/2+O(\log^*j)$ has a written derivation. The companion headlines `Rule30Submission.right_exponent` and `Rule30Submission.wall_return` bound the least dyadic exponent and give finite-width black-wall return.

This uniform result improves the exponent coefficient $2/3$ in the pinned kit's `Rule30RightPeriods.per_upper`. It also improves Nersissian's Fibonacci ceiling, whose coefficient is approximately $0.69424$.

The mechanism tracks the multiplicity at $1$ of a temporal polynomial over $\mathbf F_2$ along the black-wall map $\mathrm{PhiS}\,3$. Exposing two more bits multiplies a cycle length by $1$, $2$, or $4$. Multiplication by $4$ resets a resource exponentially, while multiplication by $2$ reduces it by at most one. An inductive record invariant yields the inverse-tower correction.

Optimality and worldwide priority are not certified. None of Prize Problems 1–3 is resolved.

entry.description:
A finite-depth right edge follows the single-cell ruler with a fixed cap. The primary source reports: For every finite nonzero row $x$ of rule 30, read from its rightmost black cell $e$ (bit $k$ of the edge code is $x(e-k)$), the edge advances one cell per step and the code evolves by the 2-adic edge map $T$ of Coven, Pivato and Yassawi (`edge_evol`). For rows of finite orbit depth, we prove the following capped-ruler theorem. Suppose the code agrees with the single cell's code at time $s_0$ on bits $0,\dots,k-1$, for some $k \ge 2$, while no code of the single cell's orbit agrees with it on bits $0,\dots,k$. Then at every time $t$ the code agrees with the single cell's code at time $s_0+t$ below bit $k$ and differs at bit $k$. Its white run behind the edge cell equals the single cell's when that run is shorter than $k-1$, is exactly $k-1$ when the single cell's is at least $k-1$, and is never longer (`frozen_ruler`). The single cell's code never has a white run of exactly $k-1$ (`no_width_at_depth`), so the cut width lies in a gap of the ruler. Every row has a depth, or agrees with the orbit at every depth (`depth_dichotomy`).

The kit's `Rule30RightPeriods` describes the single cell's right diagonals; this gives a conditional capped-ruler theorem and a depth dichotomy for arbitrary right-edge codes. The proof uses only the triangularity of $T$, with no counting of periods.

Not claimed: anything about the center column or the Prize problems, or that rows of infinite depth are the single cell's own rows (open). references.title: A finite-depth right edge follows the single-cell ruler with a fixed cap — primary dated statement/disclosure
Primary publication and scope evidence

entry.description:
Staircases near the single cell's right edge end; the rain rows keep a two-step edge patch for ever. The primary source reports: In rule 30 grown from one black cell, call a maximal alternating stretch of length at least $3$ a staircase. Its interior keeps its colors, and its front is eaten one cell per row (`front_step`), so a living staircase keeps its distance $W$ from the advancing right edge. entry.description:
A seven-cell rewrite beside the white wall that merges in two steps, for every tail and every finite cut. The primary source reports: For the kit's zero-boundary left half (`Rule30ZeroBoundary.zrow`), consider the starts $1100011\,\tau$ and $1010101\,\tau$, read from the wall outward, with the same arbitrary tail $\tau$ from depth $8$ on. We prove that their rows are equal at time $2$ (`mergePrefix_two`) and so at every later time (`mergePrefix_future`). The same holds for their truncations at any common depth $W \ge 7$ (`mergePrefix_truncate`), which are finitely supported. The depth-$7$ cell is needed: with it white and a white tail, the truncations at depth $6$ do not merge (`mergePrefix_needs_seven`).

Inside the kit's reconstruction `Theta`, take free-bit sequences $f$, $g$ that agree from index $1$ on, with $f_1 = f_2 = 1$. Then $\Theta f$ reads this prefix with $a = f_0$ (`theta_prefix`). $\Theta f$ and $\Theta g$ agree at every depth $k \ge 7$ (`theta_first_edit_local`), and their truncations at every $W \ge 7$ merge at time $2$ (`theta_truncate_merge`). The kit's `two_step_shift` already merges the untruncated $\Theta f$ and $\Theta g$; what is added is the localization, which survives a common finite cut.

Two reading lemmas are included. Merged rows have the same last black depth, by the kit's `zrow_edge` (`merge_preserves_last_black`). A merger at time $T$, together with agreement at the earlier even observations, is equivalent to trace agreement at every even time and at every time from $T$ onward (`odd_edits_iff_guarded_merge`).

entry.description:
Explicit log log margins for constant runs of the Rule 30 center. The primary source reports: For Rule 30 grown from one black cell, write $c_t$ for the center and $\ell(a)=\lfloor\log_2\lfloor\log_2 a\rfloor\rfloor$. For every $a,L\in\mathbb N$, if $a\ge16$ and $c_{a+i}=1$ for every $i<L$, then $5L+18\ell(a)\le3a+51$ (`Rule30Submission.black_run_loglog_spaced`). If $a\ge256$ and $c_{a+i}=0$ for every $i<L$, then $L+6\ell(a)\le a+17$ (`Rule30Submission.white_run_loglog_spaced`). These bounds concern every constant block, whether maximal or not, with no periodicity assumptions.

At kit commit `7d66504`, `Rule30CenterRuns` gives $L\le a$ for black runs and $L\le a-3$ for white runs when $a\ge3$. The slope $3/5$ for black runs is already public (R30-20261025-0554f7 proves $5L\le3a+10$); what is new here is an explicit margin growing like $\log\log a$, for both colors. The package also retains bounds with smaller logarithmic coefficients and different intercepts.

The method reads the single-seed history along left diagonals. Eventually white diagonals are at least five apart, and a gap of five can only start at index two. Their count controls eventual periods; injectivity of consecutive profiles forces new white diagonals. Explicit settling times turn those diagonals into barriers to long center runs.

This is a partial result related to Problem 1. It proves neither eventual nonperiodicity, density one half, nor a computation lower bound.

entry.description:
Clone-Ray Transfer Laws, the Backward 00 <-> 1^infty Avalanche Dichotomy, and Survivor Pullback Characterization for Zero-Boundary Stripe Front Windows. The primary source reports: Responding to the review on R30-20261027-1910d0, we prove five structural laws for zero-boundary stripe front windows in core Lean 4.35.0 (`Rule30ZeroBoundaryStripeStructure`, 2.42 s, 9.4 MB RAM, zero certificate tables):

1. Even-Step Orbit Invariance (`cycle_orb_even_iff`): By `universal_front_period` and `sig_congr`, `Cycle K S W p lam` is invariant along the even-step orbit of `(W, p)`.
2. entry.description: White runs beside two periodic columns of rule 30 are at most two periods long. The primary source reports: For every configuration $x : \mathbb{Z} \to \{0,1\}$ of rule 30 whose columns $0$ and $1$ are periodic with a common period $P \ge 2$ from time $0$, and whose column $0$ is black at some time, every run of white cells in row $0$ to the left of column $0$ has length at most $2P-2$ (`Rule30Submission.zero_run_le`); a white run of odd length $2m+1 \ge 3$ with black cells at both ends needs $P \ge m+3$, so it has length at most $2P-5$ (`Rule30Submission.odd_zero_run_le`). The kit propagates periodicity to the left (`Rule30Jen.periodic_left`) and, by Jen's theorem (`Rule30FiniteConfigs.jen`), the hypotheses never hold in a configuration with a leftmost black cell; we found no bound on white runs beside two periodic columns in the catalog or among the listed submissions. The proof: periodicity moves left; a long white run leaves a white triangle that makes the column at depth $d+P-1$ white for a whole period, hence for ever; the column to its right then only latches black, so being periodic and white at time $0$ it is white for ever; two adjacent white columns force white columns to their right up to column $0$. The bound is attained: on rings of up to 18 cells, the period-3 ether $(000010011111)^\infty$ has white runs of $4$ and $(0000001)^\infty$, of period $4$, has runs of $6$. The statement is vacuous for configurations with a leftmost black cell, and nothing here concerns the single-seed centre column or decides Problem 1. entry.description: The 101 shift law for the right diagonals of rule 30, with its mod-4 forms. The primary source reports: Let $q$ be even and let $d, a, b, c, z$ be Boolean profiles in time with $d(t+q)=d(t)$, $a(t+q)=\lnot a(t)$, $b(t+2q)=b(t)$ and $c(t+2q)=\lnot c(t)$, where $b(t+1)=b(t)\oplus(a(t)\lor d(t))$ and $z(t+1)=z(t)\oplus(c(t)\lor b(t))$. Then $z(t+4q)=z(t)\oplus\eta$ for every $t$, with $\eta=\mathrm{parity}(q/2)\oplus E_q(d)$ and $E_q(d)$ the XOR of $d$ at the even ticks $0,2,\dots,q-2$ (`Rule30Submission.shift_law`). On the kit's evolution the right diagonals $D_j(t)=x_t(t-j)$ of every start obey this recurrence, so the law holds on actual diagonals under the same period hypotheses (`rightDiag_shift_law`). For $q\equiv0\pmod 4$, $E_q(d)$ is a XOR of $h(4s)\oplus h(4s+1)$ for $d(t+1)=d(t)\oplus h(t)$ (`E_mod4`); if $d$ complements at $q/2$, then $\eta=\mathrm{parity}(q/2)\oplus\mathrm{parity}(q/4)$, which is false for $q\equiv0\pmod 8$ and true at $q=4$ (`eta_false_of_antiperiod`, `eta_four`); if $d$ has period $q/2$, then $\eta$ is false (`eta_false_of_period_half`). The kit already has the general doubling criterion for right diagonals (`Rule30RightPeriods.S_rule`, and the T-function lifting criterion); what is added is this explicit shift law after the doubling letters 101 and its mod-4 forms. The proof pairs ticks three times: $i$ with $i+2q$, consecutive ticks, and $k$ with $k+q/2$; a window over a full period makes the result independent of $t$. These are conditional profile statements: the translation from a finite seed's prefix-period letters to the hypotheses is derived by hand, not formalized here, so `eta_false_of_antiperiod` alone is not a kernel-checked finite-seed word exclusion. Nothing here concerns the centre column or decides Problem 1. entry.description: The universal start of the right diagonals of rule 30. The primary source reports: For a nonzero finitely supported initial row of Rule 30, translate the rightmost black cell to 0 and let m >= 2 be the first index whose adjacent leftward start bits agree. We prove that D(m+1), ..., D(m+6) have individual least periods 4, 8, 8, 16, 32, 32, and D(m+7) has least period 32 or 64. A general version assumes only right-finiteness and existence of this first equal pair. The actual Rule30Realization.evol diagonals are linked to a two-feeder recurrence with an all-time 256-period bound for the seven new profiles. A core-Lean kernel certificate checks all 256 initial assignments in sixteen groups and certifies their least periods. The companion notebook illustrates seven seeds. entry.description: Light-speed periodic rings of rule 30 as closed walks of periodic profiles. The primary source reports: Read rule 30 in the frame that moves one cell right per step, Phi x i = x i XOR (x (i+1) OR x (i+2)). Then the P-th iterate is the kit's evolution moved P cells (`Rule30Submission.orbit_eq_iff`), so Phi^P x = x says that x returns after P steps moved P cells right: velocity one, outside the range [-1, 1) that the kit's PeriodicPoints covers. A ring of size m is an m-periodic configuration. We prove that the rings of size m with Phi^P x = x correspond bijectively, by explicit inverse maps, to closed walks of length m in the graph of P-periodic profiles, where consecutive sites obey the right-diagonal recurrence (`Rule30Submission.encode_walk`, `Rule30Submission.decode_ring`, `Rule30Submission.decode_encode`, `Rule30Submission.encode_decode`). The identities hold for every P and m; their finite-graph reading needs P and m positive. At period two the classification is complete for every positive ring size: Phi^2 x = x exactly for the white ring and the alternating rings (`Rule30Submission.ring_period_two`), alternating rings have even size (`Rule30Submission.alternating_even`), and only white is fixed by Phi (`Rule30Submission.ring_fixed`). The period-two rings are therefore the restrictions of rule 30's three fixed points. No classification is claimed for larger periods, and nothing here concerns the centre column. Primary publication and scope evidence

entry.description:
The left diagonals of rule 30: their periods are unbounded, and the settled band has no long white run. The primary source reports: The catalog proves that every left diagonal $D_j(t) = c(t,\, j - t)$ of the rule 30 pattern is eventually periodic, with a period dividing $2^j$ (`Rule30Diagonals.D_periodic`). This essay proves what the periods can be. For every configuration with a leftmost black cell:

- **Lemma B1.** No two adjacent left diagonals are both eventually white, and an eventually white diagonal is followed, two later, by an eventually black one (`seed_no_adjacent_white`, `seed_white_then_black`).
- **Lemma B2.** No $P \ge 1$ is an eventual period of every left diagonal: among the first $4^P + 2$ diagonals, one does not have eventual period $P$. So the eventual periods are unbounded, and infinitely many diagonals are eventually white and infinitely many eventually black (`seed_periods_unbounded`, `seed_periods_unbounded_quant`, `seed_infinitely_many_white`, `seed_infinitely_many_black`).
- **Lemma B3.** If the diagonals $0, \dots, M$ have had a common period $P$ for $P$ steps, then a white run of the row inside them that is bounded on the left by a black diagonal has length at most $2P - 1$ (`lemma_B3_sharp`).

The unboundedness of the periods is Rowland's (2006); the proofs, the quantitative form and Lemmas B1 and B3 are new. Nothing here decides Problem 1. references.title: The left diagonals of rule 30: their periods are unbounded, and the settled band has no long white run — primary dated statement/disclosure
Primary publication and scope evidence

entry.description:
A repeat on the center column cannot put its white run inside the settled band of left diagonals. The primary source reports: Jen's theorem with a clock, the catalog's `window_jen_col`, bounds a block of length $n$ that columns $0$ and $1$ share at times $a < a_2$ by $n \le a_2$. The bound comes from a white run: row $a_2$ is white at the distances $a + 1, \dots, n - 1$ left of the center, which lie on the left diagonals $a_2 - n + 1, \dots, a_2 - a - 1$. This essay proves that the run cannot lie in the band of diagonals that has settled.

**Theorem $\mathrm{A}''''$.** If the diagonals $0, \dots, M$ agree at times $a_2 - P$ and $a_2$, with $1 \le P \le a_2$ and $M < a_2 - a$, then $n \le L + a_2 - M + 2P - 1$, for every configuration with a leftmost black cell $L$ cells left of the column (`theorem_A4_sharp`; for the single seed, with the kit's `cell` and `Rule30Diagonals.D`, `center_A4_sharp`).

entry.description:
Under a period-2 center column, a right neighbour that starts with near-squares has no left edge. The primary source reports: The first open case of Problem 1 is period 2: the center column reads the clock $0101\ldots$ from some time on. Under that clock, the left-permutivity of rule 30 determines column $-1$ from column $1$: black at odd times, and the complement of column $1$ at even times. Call column $1$ at even times the visible bits.

**Corollary F** (`Rule30Submission.corollary_F`). A configuration with a leftmost black cell whose column $0$ reads the clock from some time $T_0$ has no near-squares at unbounded scales in its visible bits: there is no constant $K$ with pairs $i < i_2$, $i_2 - i$ unbounded, whose common future lasts $i_2 - K$ steps.

The proof joins two facts proved for every configuration with a leftmost black cell: Lemma B2, that infinitely many left diagonals are eventually black (`infinitely_many_black`), and Theorem $\mathrm{A}'''$, that a black diagonal sharpens Jen's clocked bound on a block shared by two adjacent columns (`theorem_A3`). The visible agreement gives columns $-1$ and $0$ a common block of length $2(i_2 - K)$, and an eventually black diagonal $b \ge L + 2K$ bounds it by $2i_2 - 2K - 1$.

The essay checks the period-doubling word, whose first $2^k$ bits recur at $2^k$ for exactly $2^k - 1$ bits, and computes its forced left half: black cells at every depth up to $2995$ and beyond, as the theorem says. entry.description:
Q001 up to Width 37, and the Words 0^(P-1)1 of Rule 30. The primary source reports: The catalog reduces the period-3 word $001$ to `Q001`, an open statement about the zero-boundary left half: no start with a leftmost black cell keeps column $-1$ black at every third step. Its only evidence so far was a search in C.

This essay generalizes the catalog's bit-sliced kernel checker for `Q01` from the even steps to the multiples of any period $P$, with its soundness proof, and proves in the Lean kernel that

- `Q001` holds for every start of width at most $37$ (`q001_width_le_37`, `q001_restricted`);
- its analog $Q_P$ for $P = 5$ holds up to width $28$ (`q00001_width_le_28`).

It also states the reduction uniformly: for every $P \ge 2$, $Q_P$ excludes $(0^{P-1}1)^\infty$ as a tail of the center column, whatever the transient (`not_eventually_oneBlack_of_QP`). For $P = 2$ and $3$ this is the catalog's route; for $P = 4$ the catalog's C3 reduction is sharper, and $P = 11, 12, 13$ are already excluded outright, so the uniform reduction is new only for the other $P \ge 5$.

$Q_P$ stays open for every $P$; the bounded cases are finite evidence. entry.description:
Rule 210 beside the period-2 clock: the one-sided question is false and the left half is linear. The primary source reports: The catalog's `Rule30ZeroBoundary.Q01` is the period-2 question for rule 30 in one-sided form: no finitely supported start of the zero-boundary left half keeps column $-1$ black at every even step. Its barrier `Rule30Realization.barrier` shows that left-permutivity, the moving edge and Jen's theorem cannot decide Problem 1 alone, since rules 90, 150 and 210 share them. This essay asks the same question of rule 210, $x' = \ell \oplus (\lnot c \land r)$, the sibling that, like rule 30, is nonlinear and not right-permutive.

**For rule 210 the one-sided statement is false** (`not_Q01_210`): the empty start keeps the clock for ever. The reason is a parity invariant (`parity_invariant`): for every start consistent with the clock, every black cell at time $t$ and depth $k$ has $t + k$ even. So no two horizontally adjacent cells are both black, the gate $\lnot c \land r$ reduces to $r$, and the left half evolves as rule 90 does, linearly (`linear`).

The essay also computes the empty start's run, its parity, the bits of column $1$ it forces (runs of doubling lengths), and the number of starts of width $W$ that survive $W$ steps: $2^{\lfloor W/2 \rfloor}$, the same count as the catalog's `count_constrained` for rule 30. The two-sided statement, that no finite configuration keeps rule 210's clock, has a proof by hand that is not formalized here. Nothing here decides Problem 1. entry.description:
Every Sturmian word, of every slope and every intercept, is excluded as the right neighbour of a period-2 center column. The primary source reports: For every irrational slope $0 \le \alpha < 1$ and every intercept $\theta$, the mechanical word $m_{\alpha,\theta}(i) = \lfloor \theta + (i+1)\alpha \rfloor - \lfloor \theta + i\alpha \rfloor$ is not the sequence of visible bits of any configuration with a leftmost black cell $L \ge 1$ cells left of the center whose center column reads the clock $0101\ldots$ from some time $T_0$ on: $\mathrm{evol}\,x_0\,(2i)\,1 = m_{\alpha,\theta}(i)$ for all $i$ is impossible (`Rule30Submission.sturmian_excluded`; the clock from time $0$ without the condition on $L$, `sturmian_excluded_clock0`; the fractional-part form $m(i) = [1 - \alpha \le \{\theta + i\alpha\}]$, `sturmian_excluded_fract`). The same holds for every block code of the word (`sturmian_block_excluded`).

The catalog reduces period 2 to `Rule30ZeroBoundary.Q01` and says nothing about the right neighbour of a clocked center column. Our submission R30-20261023-0c4a33 excluded the characteristic words, intercept $0$, through the standard words; this essay removes that restriction with a combinatorial argument.

A Sturmian word has at most $n + 1$ distinct blocks of length $n$, so two of the $n + 2$ blocks starting at positions $0, \ldots, n + 1$ coincide (`exists_block_collision`, by the pigeonhole principle on threshold sets); irrationality keeps the two positions far apart as $n$ grows (`no_small_period`), which gives near-squares with slack $1$ at unbounded scales (`sturmian_pairs`). Shifting the intercept by $T_0 \alpha$ moves the clock's start to time $0$, and Corollary F (R30-20261022-91b0b0) forbids such near-squares.

Nothing is claimed for rational slopes, nor for any right neighbour that is not a block code of a Sturmian word.
